title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad
openingText: The Nellie, a cruising yawl, turned on her anchor, her sails never stirring, and came to rest. The flood tide had begun to flow, and the wind had almost died. Since we were heading downriver, we could only anchor there and wait for the tide to turn.
about:
On a boat anchored in the Thames, Marlow tells his companions about a job with a European trading company in Africa. His journey upriver brings him into a world of forced labour, waste and obsessive pursuit of ivory. Before he meets the celebrated agent Kurtz, he hears competing accounts of the man's talents and ambitions.

First published in 1899, the story draws on Conrad's journey to the Congo in 1890. It exposes colonial violence through a narrator whose own language and assumptions also demand scrutiny. Marlow's hesitations, digressions and repeated images make this a story about the difficulty of understanding and telling an experience, as well as about what happened.

angleCards.title: Who is telling the story?
angleCards.text: An unnamed listener recounts Marlow's account. Notice where Marlow admits uncertainty, interrupts himself or anticipates objections from his listeners.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow how the two narrators shape what I know, and where Marlow's judgments remain uncertain.

angleCards.title: Trade and its justifications
angleCards.text: Compare the Company's claims about progress with the labour, violence and waste Marlow describes. Ask whose interests its rules serve.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to compare colonial rhetoric with what happens at the stations and along the river.

angleCards.title: The making of Kurtz
angleCards.text: Kurtz first appears through other people's words. Track their different interests and expectations before comparing those accounts with his appearance.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace how Kurtz's reputation is constructed and what happens when Marlow meets him.

angleCards.title: Who gets a voice?
angleCards.text: Marlow describes African people through racial categories and often interprets their words and actions for them. Notice where the narrative grants or withholds speech and individuality.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine both the criticism of colonialism and the limits of the narrator's recognition of African humanity.

cast.name: Marlow
cast.description: A sailor recalling his work as a steamboat captain. He tries to explain both the journey and the lasting disturbance it caused him.

cast.name: Kurtz
cast.description: A highly praised ivory agent whose eloquence, ambitions and power become the focus of Marlow's journey.

cast.name: The Company
cast.description: The unnamed European trading organisation that employs Marlow and Kurtz. Its offices, stations and employees reveal the gap between its claims and its practices.

cast.name: The Manager
cast.description: An administrator whose endurance and concern for his own position matter more than any evident talent. His attitude to Kurtz combines professional concern and rivalry.

cast.name: The frame narrator
cast.description: The unnamed man aboard the Nellie who introduces Marlow's story and returns to the Thames at its close.

whyItMatters.title: Colonial power and responsibility
whyItMatters.body: The story sets claims about civilisation beside coercion, suffering and the pursuit of profit. Its officials often turn questions of responsibility into questions of procedure. Read their language alongside the people and consequences it excludes.

whyItMatters.title: A story that questions its own telling
whyItMatters.body: Marlow repeatedly struggles to convey what an experience meant. The frame narrative, interruptions and recurring images prevent his account from becoming a simple report. Readers must consider what he reveals, what he cannot express and what he may fail to recognise.

whyItMatters.title: Achebe's challenge
whyItMatters.body: In a 1975 lecture at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, Chinua Achebe challenged the story's portrayal of Africa and Africans. His criticism remains a useful question to bring to the text: can a work expose colonial cruelty while also denying the people it describes a full voice?
